stages.name: Analysis
stages.summary: Working out what the solution must do and the conditions it must work within. The team gathers data about the problem, need or opportunity, usually from the people involved, and from it identifies the solution requirements, constraints and scope; in Software Development these are documented in a software requirements specification (SRS). Analysis settles *what* the solution must do, not *how*.

activities.name: Solution requirements
activities.summary: Determining the functional requirements, which say what the solution must do (the input it needs, the output it produces and its functions, including how it manipulates and validates data), and the non-functional requirements, which are quality attributes such as usability, reliability, portability, robustness and maintainability. Context diagrams, data flow diagrams and use case diagrams help work them out.

activities.name: Solution constraints
activities.summary: Identifying the conditions and limits the design must take into account: economic (cost and time), technical (such as processing speed, capacity, available equipment, compatibility and security), social (the users' level of expertise), legal (intellectual property, and the ownership and privacy of data) and usability (accessibility, usefulness and ease of use).

activities.name: Solution scope
activities.summary: Setting the boundaries of the solution by stating what it will address and what it will not, for example features left for a later version.

activities.name: Skills underpinning the analysis stage
activities.summary: Collecting data with a range of techniques, such as interviews, observations, surveys and reports, to find out and clarify what users need; judging how reliable, valid and relevant the data and its sources are; and drafting questions, with follow-up questions, that probe the problem, need or opportunity.

stages.name: Design
stages.summary: Planning how the solution will work and look before any code is written. The team generates design ideas, develops evaluation criteria and uses them to choose a preferred idea, then develops that idea into detailed designs of the solution's data, functionality, appearance and user interface. The same criteria are later used to evaluate the finished solution.

activities.name: Solution design
activities.summary: Developing design ideas into a preferred, detailed design using design principles and design tools. Ideation tools such as mood boards, brainstorming, mind maps, sketches and annotations generate the ideas; tools such as data dictionaries, mock-ups, object descriptions, IPO charts and pseudocode then set out the data the solution needs (its names, structure, validation and processing), its functionality and its appearance.

activities.name: Skills underpinning the design stage
activities.summary: Investigating existing and possible solutions, generating design ideas and showing how they connect with text and diagrams, producing detailed annotated designs of appearance and functionality from those ideas, and planning contingencies for issues that could affect the design.

activities.name: Evaluation criteria
activities.summary: Developing criteria, based on the requirements, that measure efficiency and effectiveness. They are first used to judge how well the design ideas meet the requirements, are refined as the solution develops, and are used again to judge the finished solution.

stages.name: Development
stages.summary: Building the solution from the requirements and designs. The team codes it in a programming language, validates its input data, tests and debugs it to make sure it meets the requirements, and writes internal documentation.

activities.name: Manipulation
activities.summary: Coding the solution to meet its specifications with suitable algorithms and features of the programming language, and applying formats and conventions that improve its appearance.

activities.name: Validation
activities.summary: Checking that input data is reasonable and complete, for example with existence, type and range checks. Validation can be manual or electronic, and testing shows whether it works.

activities.name: Testing
activities.summary: Checking that the solution meets its requirements, works as expected and can be used by its intended users: using debugging techniques, planning a testing strategy (the features to test, the test data and the expected results), running the tests, comparing actual with expected results and correcting the errors found.

activities.name: Documentation
activities.summary: Writing internal documentation, such as comments in the code, that explains how the solution is built and how it behaves, so that it can be maintained and upgraded.

activities.name: Skills underpinning the development stage
activities.summary: While the solution is being built: modifying and evolving the designs, refining the evaluation criteria, and planning contingencies for issues that arise along the way.

stages.name: Evaluation
stages.summary: Judging how well the finished solution meets its requirements once it has been developed and put into use. The team prepares an evaluation strategy, then applies the evaluation criteria to the data collected and discusses the solution's efficiency and effectiveness.

activities.name: Evaluation strategy
activities.summary: Planning how the solution will be evaluated once it is developed and in use: the evaluation criteria, the time frame, the data to collect and the methods for collecting it, who is responsible for collecting it, and how the data relates to each criterion.

activities.name: Solution evaluation
activities.summary: Applying the evaluation criteria to the data collected to decide how well the solution meets the requirements, needs or opportunities, and discussing its efficiency and effectiveness.

activities.name: Skills underpinning the evaluation stage
activities.summary: Looking back critically at how the analysis and design processes helped meet the requirements, and identifying improvements that a different approach to the problem-solving methodology could have brought.

specifications: Analysis: the functional requirements state what the solution must do: the input it needs, the output it produces and its functions, including how it manipulates and validates data.
Analysis: the non-functional requirements state the quality attributes the solution must have, such as usability, reliability, portability, robustness and maintainability.
Analysis: context diagrams, data flow diagrams and use case diagrams are used to help determine the solution requirements.

Analysis: the constraints set out what the design must take into account: economic (cost and time), technical (such as processing speed, capacity, equipment, compatibility and security), social (users' expertise), legal (intellectual property and the ownership and privacy of data) and usability (accessibility, usefulness and ease of use).
Analysis: the scope marks the boundaries of the solution, saying what it will address and what it will not.

Analysis: data is collected with a range of techniques, its sources are checked for reliability, validity and relevance, and questions and follow-up questions are prepared to clarify needs and requirements.

Analysis: the findings are documented in a software requirements specification (SRS) that describes the functional and non-functional requirements, constraints, scope, user characteristics and technical environments.
Design: the design lists the data the solution needs and plans its names, structure, validation and processing, showing how the solution will work and look.

Design: design ideas are generated with ideation tools such as mood boards, brainstorming, mind maps, sketches and annotations, and the preferred idea is developed into detailed designs using design principles.
Design: design tools such as data dictionaries, IPO charts, object descriptions and pseudocode show the solution's structure and functionality.

Design: annotated diagrams and mock-ups show how the solution's components relate and lay out its interface, giving the position and size of text and images, fonts and styles, colours and text enhancements.
Design: existing and possible solutions are investigated, ideas are connected with text and diagrams, detailed annotated designs are produced, and contingencies are planned for likely issues.
Design: evaluation criteria are developed to judge how well the designs meet the requirements; the same criteria are later used to judge the finished solution's efficiency and effectiveness.
Development: the solution is coded to meet its specifications with suitable algorithms and programming language features, and formats and conventions are applied to improve its appearance.
Development: validation, including existence, type and range checks, confirms that input data is reasonable and complete.

Development: a testing strategy lists the features to be tested, the test data and the expected results; the tests are run, actual results are recorded and compared with the expected results, and errors are debugged and corrected.
Development: internal documentation in the code explains how the solution works, so that it can be kept running, maintained and upgraded.
Development: while the solution is being built, the designs are modified and evolved, the evaluation criteria are refined, and contingencies are planned for issues that arise.

Evaluation: an evaluation strategy sets out how the solution will be evaluated once it is in use: the evaluation criteria, the time frame, the data to be collected and how, who is responsible for collecting it, and how the data relates to each criterion.
Evaluation: the solution evaluation applies the evaluation criteria to the data to judge how well the solution meets the requirements, and discusses its efficiency and effectiveness.

Evaluation: the analysis and design processes are critically reviewed for how well they helped meet the requirements, and improvements from approaching the problem-solving methodology differently are identified.

cards.back: A structured approach to creating a software solution in four stages: analysis, design, development and evaluation. Each stage has its own activities, and each stage builds on the work of the one before it.

cards.front: The four stages of the problem-solving methodology, in order, are {{analysis}}, {{design}}, {{development}} and {{evaluation}}.
cards.back: Each stage relies on the one before it: design ideas are judged against the requirements found in analysis, the code is built from the detailed design, and evaluation needs a finished solution that has been in use.
cards.mistake: Testing is not a stage of its own. It is an activity inside the development stage.

cards.back: The PSM stage that works out *what* the solution must do. The team investigates the problem, need or opportunity and documents the functional and non-functional requirements, the constraints and the scope.
cards.mistake: Analysis doesn't decide how the solution will look or work. Screen layouts and algorithms belong to design.

cards.back: The PSM stage that plans *how* the solution will work and look. Its activities are **solution design**, in which design ideas are generated and the preferred one is developed into detailed designs with design principles and design tools, and **evaluation criteria**, which judge how well the designs meet the requirements and are used again to evaluate the finished solution.
cards.mistake: Evaluating design ideas happens here, in design. It is not part of the evaluation stage.

cards.back: The PSM stage that builds a working solution from the requirements and designs. Its activities are **manipulation** (coding it with suitable algorithms and programming language features), **validation** of input data, **testing** (including debugging and correcting errors) and **documentation**, which in Software Development means internal documentation.
cards.mistake: Validation and testing both happen in development, but they aren't the same. Validation checks that input data is reasonable and complete, usually through checks built into the program; testing checks that the solution, including its validation, meets the requirements and works as expected.

cards.back: The PSM stage that judges how well the finished solution meets its requirements. Its activities are the **evaluation strategy**, which plans the criteria, time frame, data and responsibility (best before launch, so data such as old-system task times can be gathered), and **solution evaluation**, which applies the criteria after a period of use to judge efficiency and effectiveness.
cards.mistake: Evaluation isn't a final round of testing. It asks how well the solution serves its users, not whether each module gives the right output.

cards.back:
| Aspect | Testing | Evaluation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Stage | Development | Evaluation |
| Asks | Does it work as intended? | How efficient and effective is it? |
| When | While it is being built | After a period of real use |
| Checked against | Expected output | Evaluation criteria |
cards.mistake: Re-running the test table after launch isn't an evaluation. Evaluation measures the solution in real use against the criteria set in design.

cards.front: Evaluating design ideas versus evaluating the solution
cards.back: **Design ideas** are evaluated in the *design* stage: the evaluation criteria are applied to each idea so the preferred design can be chosen before development starts. The **solution** is evaluated in the *evaluation* stage: the same criteria, refined while the solution was built, judge how efficient and effective the finished solution is.
cards.mistake: An activity with 'evaluate' in its name isn't automatically in the evaluation stage. Comparing design ideas is a design activity.

cards.front: Evaluation criteria are set in the {{design}} stage and applied in the {{evaluation}} stage.
cards.back: The criteria come from the requirements. In design they are used to choose the preferred design idea, they can be refined while the solution is developed, and the same criteria then judge how efficient and effective the finished solution is.
cards.mistake: Criteria aren't written once the solution is finished. Criteria chosen at the end tend to fit whatever the solution already does.

cards.front: What should a detailed design show, and why?
cards.back: The preferred design's appearance (for example, mock-ups) and its structure and functionality (for example, a data dictionary, object descriptions, IPO charts or pseudocode), in enough detail that a developer could code the solution without guessing what was intended.
cards.mistake: A single sketch of the main screen isn't a detailed design. It says nothing about the data or the processing.

cards.front: Why does analysis come before design?
cards.back: Design ideas can only be judged against the requirements, constraints and scope. Without them, the team could design and build something that doesn't meet the need, and a mistake found late costs far more to fix than one found on paper.

cards.front: Collecting data in analysis versus collecting data in evaluation
cards.back: In **analysis**, data (for example, from interviews, surveys or observation) shows what users need and what is wrong with the current situation. In **evaluation**, data shows how well the finished solution meets the evaluation criteria.
cards.mistake: A survey doesn't belong to one stage. Ask what the data is for: finding requirements (analysis) or judging the finished solution (evaluation).

cards.front: Analysis works out {{what}} the solution must do; design works out {{how}} it will do it.
cards.back: 'Record each booking' is a requirement from analysis. The mock-up of the booking screen and the pseudocode that saves a booking come from design.

cards.front: What does an evaluation report do?
cards.back: It applies each evaluation criterion to the data collected under the evaluation strategy and states, with evidence, how efficient and effective the solution is.
cards.mistake: A report that lists the solution's features, or says users 'liked it', without data for each criterion hasn't evaluated anything.

cards.front: In which PSM stage are context diagrams, data flow diagrams and use case diagrams mainly used, and why?
cards.back: Analysis. The PSM lists them as tools for determining the solution requirements: they show the system's boundary, the data moving in and out of it, and how users interact with it. It also lists them among the design tools that show how a solution's components relate.

mcq.stem: Farid's team is building a rostering program for an aged care home in Warrnambool. This week the team is surveying care staff about the problems they have with the current paper rosters. Which stage of the problem-solving methodology is the team working in?
options: Analysis
Design
Development
Evaluation
mcq.explanation: The team is collecting data about the current system to find out what staff need. Investigating the problem to work out the requirements is analysis.
whyWrong: Design plans how the solution will look and work, which can't start until the requirements are known.
Development builds and tests the program, which can't start until there is a design to build from.
Evaluation surveys users about the finished solution, but this survey is about the current paper rosters.

mcq.stem: Tomás has sketched three possible home screens for a volunteer sign-up app for an animal shelter in Bendigo. He scores each sketch against criteria such as 'a volunteer can see this week's open shifts without scrolling', then chooses the highest-scoring sketch. Which activity is Tomás carrying out?
options: Evaluating the solution, in the evaluation stage
Evaluating design ideas, in the design stage
Testing the interface, in the development stage
Determining requirements, in the analysis stage
mcq.explanation: Tomás is comparing alternative designs against criteria to choose a preferred one before anything is built. That is evaluating design ideas, a design activity.
whyWrong: The evaluation stage judges a finished solution in use, and these are only sketches.
Testing runs a built program with test data, and nothing has been coded yet.
Requirements say what the app must do; Tomás is choosing how it will look.

mcq.stem: A stock program for a Geelong hardware store has a range check on its quantity field. Mei Lin types a quantity of -3, checks that an error message appears, and records the result in a test table. Which activity is Mei Lin carrying out?
options: Validation, because the program is checking the input it receives
Evaluation, because she is judging how effective the program is
Design, because she is deciding what range the quantity must be in
Testing, because she is checking actual output against expected output
mcq.explanation: The range check in the program is validation, but Mei Lin's own task is different: she runs test data through the program and records whether the expected error message appears. That is testing, a development activity.
whyWrong: The program validates the input, but Mei Lin's task of trying an input and recording the result is testing.
Evaluation judges the finished solution in real use against evaluation criteria, not single inputs in a test table.
The allowed range was decided earlier; she is checking that the code enforces it.

mcq.stem: Two months after a Torquay physiotherapy clinic started using its new booking program, the practice manager compares the average time taken to make a booking with the time recorded for the old system, as the clinic's plan set out. Which stage of the problem-solving methodology is she working in?
options: Analysis, because she is collecting data about how bookings are made
Development, because she is testing how quickly the program runs
Evaluation, because she is judging the program in use against a criterion
Design, because she is comparing the old system with the new one
mcq.explanation: The program has been in use for two months, and she is collecting planned data to judge it against a criterion (the time taken to make a booking). That is evaluation.
whyWrong: Analysis collects data to find requirements before a solution exists, but this program is already in use.
Testing happens before release with test data; she is measuring real use two months later.
Design compares ideas before coding; she is judging a finished solution.

mcq.stem: Which sequence of activities follows the order of the problem-solving methodology?
options: Determine requirements, code the solution, evaluate design ideas, report against criteria
Evaluate design ideas, determine requirements, code the solution, report against criteria
Determine requirements, evaluate design ideas, code the solution, report against criteria
Determine requirements, evaluate design ideas, report against criteria, code the solution
mcq.explanation: Requirements come from analysis, design ideas are evaluated in design, coding happens in development, and reporting against the evaluation criteria happens in evaluation.
whyWrong: Design ideas are evaluated before coding, so that the chosen design can guide the code.
Design ideas can only be judged against the requirements, so the requirements must come first.
A report on the solution needs a finished solution, so coding must come before it.

mcq.stem: The evaluation criteria for a solution are mainly based on the output of which activity?
options: Determining the solution requirements, in the analysis stage
Generating design ideas, in the design stage
Testing modules against test tables, in the development stage
Collecting user feedback, in the evaluation stage
mcq.explanation: Evaluation criteria check whether the solution does what it was meant to do, and what it was meant to do is set out in the requirements determined in analysis.
whyWrong: Design ideas are themselves judged against criteria; they don't define what success looks like.
Testing checks that the program works as intended; it doesn't define the evaluation criteria.
Feedback is data that the criteria are applied to, not the source of the criteria.

mcq.stem: Hana's team is building an ordering app for a Ballarat bakery. Which of these documents would the team produce in the design stage?
options: A test table showing expected and actual totals for five orders
A list of constraints, including the fixed budget and the deadline
A report comparing order times before and after the app's launch
A mock-up of the order screen with each control labelled
mcq.explanation: A mock-up shows the planned appearance of the solution, which is part of the detailed design produced in the design stage.
whyWrong: Test tables record testing, which happens in development.
Constraints are identified in analysis, before design begins.
Comparing performance after launch belongs in the evaluation report.

mcq.stem: A fruit growers' co-operative in Mildura is having a program developed to record deliveries from its members. Which activity belongs to the analysis stage?
options: Stating that the program will record deliveries but not pay members
Drawing a mock-up of the delivery entry screen for the weighbridge
Writing a range check that rejects a delivery weight of zero
Surveying members about the program a month after it goes live
mcq.explanation: Deciding what the program will and won't do sets its scope, which is defined in analysis.
whyWrong: A mock-up plans the solution's appearance, which is a design activity.
Coding a validation check is a development activity.
Surveying users about the finished program is part of evaluation.

mcq.stem: A student argues that because every module of a solution produced its expected output during testing, the evaluation stage is no longer needed. Why is the student wrong?
options: Testing takes place in design, so its results can't be used to judge the solution
Testing checks the solution works; evaluation judges how efficient and effective it is in use
Evaluation repeats the tests with a larger set of test data to confirm the earlier results
Evaluation is needed only when testing has found errors that the developers didn't fix
mcq.explanation: Correct output doesn't show that the solution is efficient or effective for its users. Evaluation measures the solution in real use against the evaluation criteria.
whyWrong: Testing is a development activity, not a design one.
Evaluation isn't retesting; it measures the solution in real use against the evaluation criteria.
Every solution is evaluated, even one with no known errors, because correct output isn't the same as meeting users' needs.

mcq.stem: A Shepparton transport company will start using a new timesheet program next month. Before it goes live, Grace writes down that she will export the program's error logs in week six and interview three supervisors in week eight. Which activity is Grace carrying out?
options: Setting evaluation criteria, in the design stage
Collecting data about needs, in the analysis stage
Planning the evaluation strategy, in the evaluation stage
Writing a test plan, in the development stage
mcq.explanation: Grace is planning what data will be collected, how and when, so the program can be judged later. That plan is the evaluation strategy.
whyWrong: Criteria say what success looks like; Grace is planning how and when the data will be gathered.
Analysis collects data before a solution exists; Grace is planning to study a finished program in use.
A test plan checks that the program works before release; Grace is planning how to judge it in use.

mcq.stem: While coding a quote calculator for a pool builder in Sale, Jonah adds a comment above a function explaining why the pool's surface area is rounded up to whole square metres. Which stage and activity is this?
options: Design: producing pseudocode for the detailed design
Development: writing internal documentation
Development: writing user documentation
Evaluation: reporting on the solution's efficiency
mcq.explanation: A comment in the code that justifies a processing choice is internal documentation, written for developers while the solution is being coded.
whyWrong: Pseudocode plans the algorithm before coding; Jonah is commenting code he has already written.
User documentation explains how to operate the program; users never read comments in the code.
An evaluation report judges the finished solution in use, not individual lines of code.

mcq.stem: Three of these activities belong to the same stage of the problem-solving methodology. Which activity belongs to a different stage?
options: Writing a validation check for the date of birth field
Recording actual output in a test table for the login module
Writing comments in the code that explain each module's purpose
Producing a data dictionary for the data the program will store
mcq.explanation: A data dictionary that plans the data to be stored is a detailed design tool, so producing it is a design activity. The other three are development activities: validation, testing and internal documentation.
whyWrong: Coding a validation check is a development activity, like two of the other options.
Recording test results is testing, a development activity.
Comments in the code are internal documentation, which is written in development.

mcq.stem: Kiri's team generated four design ideas for a loans app for a Horsham library, evaluated them, and chose a preferred idea. Which activity should the team carry out next?
options: Generate more design ideas to compare with the preferred one
Define the scope of the solution for the library's approval
Produce a detailed design of the preferred idea
Code the solution directly from the preferred idea
mcq.explanation: A chosen idea is still only an outline. The next step is to develop it into a detailed design that a developer can code from.
whyWrong: The team has already compared a range of ideas and chosen one; more ideas would repeat that work.
Scope is defined in analysis, before any design ideas are generated.
Coding needs a detailed design first; an idea on its own leaves too much for the developer to guess.

short.prompt:
Zara is developing an online booking program for a veterinary clinic in Wodonga. Classify each of the following activities by the stage of the problem-solving methodology in which it takes place.

1. Interviewing reception staff about how appointments are booked now.
2. Drawing a mock-up of the screen clients will use to choose an appointment time.
3. Entering a booking date in the past to check that it is rejected, and recording the result in a test table.
4. Surveying clients three months after launch about how easy the program is to use.

points.text: Activity 1: analysis (collecting data about the current system to find the requirements).
Activity 2: design (a mock-up is part of the detailed design).
Activity 3: development (testing that the validation works as intended).
Activity 4: evaluation (collecting data about the solution in use).

short.model:
1. Analysis: Zara is collecting data about how the clinic books appointments now, to find out what the program must do.
2. Design: the mock-up plans how the booking screen will look before it is coded.
3. Development: entering a past date and recording the result is testing, which checks that the validation works as intended.
4. Evaluation: surveying clients after three months of use collects data to judge the program against the evaluation criteria.
short.mistake: Surveys and interviews aren't always analysis. Activity 4 is a survey, but it asks about the finished program in use, so it is evaluation.

short.prompt:
Zara has developed an online booking program for a veterinary clinic in Wodonga. The clinic's practice manager plans to evaluate the program on its launch day by re-running the test table Zara used during development.

Explain two weaknesses in this plan.

points.text: Re-running the test table only shows that the program still gives the expected output, that is, that it works as intended (testing).
It doesn't measure how efficient and effective the program is against the evaluation criteria, e.g. whether clients book faster or make fewer booking errors.
On launch day, staff and clients have not yet had time to become familiar with the program.
So there is no meaningful data from real use yet; the evaluation should take place after the program has been in use for a period, e.g. a few months.

short.model: First, the test table only checks that the program produces the expected output, which Zara already confirmed during development. It says nothing about how efficient and effective the program is for the clinic, such as whether clients can book an appointment faster or with fewer errors than before, which is what the evaluation criteria measure. Second, on launch day the reception staff and clients haven't had time to become familiar with the program, so any data collected would mostly reflect their unfamiliarity. The evaluation should take place after the program has been in use for a few months, when there is enough real booking data to apply each criterion.
short.mistake: Testing and evaluation aren't interchangeable. Testing checks that the program works; evaluation judges how well it serves its users after a period of real use.
